section.title: Authority, the Tenants, and the Questions
section.sectionRationale: In the temple the leaders challenge Jesus' authority, and He answers with a question about John that traps them, then tells the parable of the wicked tenants who kill the owner's beloved son, naming Himself the rejected stone become the cornerstone. A series of hostile questions follows, on taxes to Caesar, on the resurrection, and on the Christ as David's Lord, and Jesus answers each with such wisdom that they dare ask no more. He closes by warning the crowd against the scribes who devour widows' houses and love display.
section.thesis: Jesus teaches in the temple as the Lord of it, exposing the leaders who reject Him as the murderous tenants and revealing Himself as the rejected cornerstone, the Lord of Caesar and of the living God of resurrection, David's Lord as well as David's son.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the challenge to Jesus' authority; the parable of the wicked tenants and the cornerstone; the question about taxes to Caesar; the Sadducees on the resurrection; and the Christ as David's Lord, with a warning against the scribes.

units.label: The challenge to Jesus' authority
units.note: by what authority are You doing these things

verses.text: One day as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple courts and proclaiming the gospel, the chief priests and scribes, together with the elders, came up to Him.
“Tell us,” they said, “by what {{exousia|authority}} are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?”
“I will also ask you a question,” Jesus replied. “Tell Me:
John’s baptism, was it from heaven, or from men?”
They deliberated among themselves and said, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why did you not believe him?’
But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.”
So they answered that they did not know where it was from.
And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”

units.label: The parable of the wicked tenants
units.note: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone

verses.text: Then He proceeded to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, rented it out to some tenants, and went away for a long time.
At harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat the servant and sent him away empty-handed.
So he sent another servant, but they beat him and treated him shamefully, sending him away empty-handed.
Then he sent a third, but they wounded him and threw him out.
‘What shall I do?’ asked the owner of the vineyard. ‘I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him.’
But when the tenants saw the son, they discussed it among themselves and said, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’
So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?
He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” And when the people heard this, they said, “May such a thing never happen!”
But Jesus looked directly at them and said, “Then what is the meaning of that which is written: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the {{kephalegonias|cornerstone}}’?
Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.”

units.label: Paying taxes to Caesar
units.note: give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's

verses.text: When the scribes and chief priests realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them, they sought to arrest Him that very hour. But they were afraid of the people.
So they watched Him closely and sent spies who pretended to be sincere. They were hoping to catch Him in His words in order to hand Him over to the rule and authority of the governor.
“Teacher,” they inquired, “we know that You speak and teach correctly. You show no partiality but teach the way of God in accordance with the truth.
Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?”
But Jesus saw through their duplicity and said to them,
“Show Me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” “Caesar’s,” they answered.
So Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people. And amazed at His answer, they fell silent.

units.label: The Sadducees and the resurrection
units.note: He is not the God of the dead, but of the living

verses.text: Then some of the Sadducees, who say there is no {{anastasis|resurrection}}, came to question Him.
“Teacher,” they said, “Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, the man is to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him.
Now there were seven brothers. The first one married a wife but died childless.
Then the second
and the third married the widow, and in the same way all seven died, leaving no children.
And last of all, the woman died.
So then, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her.”
Jesus answered, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage.
But those who are considered worthy to share in the age to come and in the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage.
In fact, they can no longer die, because they are like the angels. And since they are sons of the resurrection, they are sons of God.
Even Moses demonstrates that the dead are raised, in the passage about the burning bush. For he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’
He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive.”
Some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, You have spoken well!”
And they did not dare to question Him any further.

units.label: David's Lord and a warning against the scribes
units.note: David calls Him Lord, so how can He be David's son

verses.text: Then Jesus declared, “How can it be said that the Christ is the Son of David?
For David himself says in the book of Psalms: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand
until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’
Thus David calls Him ‘{{kyrios|Lord}}.’ So how can He be David’s son?”
In the hearing of all the people, Jesus said to His disciples,
“Beware of the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, and they love the greetings in the marketplaces, the chief seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets.
They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.”

exousia.gloss: Authority, the right and power to act. The leaders demand to know by what authority Jesus teaches and cleanses the temple. He answers with a question about John that exposes their bad faith, for the real issue is whether they will submit to the authority of heaven that stands before them in Him.

kephalegonias.gloss: The head of the corner, the cornerstone. Quoting Psalm 118, Jesus applies to Himself the stone the builders rejected which becomes the chief cornerstone. The builders are the leaders who reject Him; God overturns their verdict and makes the rejected Son the foundation of His new house.

anastasis.gloss: Resurrection, a rising up. The Sadducees deny it, but Jesus proves it from Moses himself: God calls Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths, and He is the God of the living. The resurrection is not a puzzle to be mocked but the promise of a God to whom all His people are alive.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master. In Psalm 110 David calls the Messiah his Lord, which means the Christ is more than merely David's descendant; He is David's Lord, exalted at God's right hand. Jesus points to His own divine identity, the Son of David who is also the Lord of David.

basic.context: Teaching in the temple, Jesus is confronted by the chief priests, scribes, and elders demanding to know by what authority He acts. He answers with a counter-question about John's baptism that leaves them trapped, refusing to say. Then He tells of a vineyard owner whose tenants beat his servants and finally kill his beloved son to seize the inheritance; the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others. Jesus names Himself the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone. His enemies send spies to trap Him on paying taxes to Caesar, and He answers, give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. The Sadducees pose a riddle to mock the resurrection, and He proves it from Moses: God is the God of the living. Then He asks how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord, and warns the crowd against the proud, widow-devouring scribes.
basic.hermeneutics: The scene is a series of confrontations in which the leaders try to trap Jesus and fail, revealing His authority and their unbelief. The parable is the interpretive center: they are the tenants who reject the Son. The questions that follow show Jesus as Lord over Caesar, over death, and over David himself, silencing every challenge.
basic.originalLanguages: The leaders demand His exousia, authority, but will not own the authority of heaven before them. Jesus names Himself the kephale gonias, the cornerstone the builders rejected. He proves the anastasis, resurrection, from Moses, since God is God of the living. And He shows that the Christ is David's kyrios, Lord, not merely his son.
basic.typology: The vineyard is Israel from Isaiah's song, its tenants the faithless leaders, its rejected son the Messiah. The rejected stone become cornerstone, from Psalm 118, is fulfilled in Christ crucified and raised. The God of the burning bush, God of the living patriarchs, guarantees the resurrection Jesus embodies.
basic.christ: Jesus is the beloved Son sent last to the vineyard and killed by the tenants, the rejected stone God makes the cornerstone. He is Lord over Caesar's realm and God's, the One who proves and will enact the resurrection, and David's Lord seated at God's right hand, the Christ who is more than a son of David.
basic.god: God is the patient owner who sends servant after servant and at last His beloved Son, and the just Lord who will not leave the tenants unpunished. He is the God of the living, to whom Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are alive, and the God who exalts His rejected Son to His right hand.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 5 is the song of the vineyard behind the parable. Psalm 118 gives the rejected stone made cornerstone. Exodus 3 is the burning bush Jesus cites for the resurrection. Psalm 110 is David calling the Christ his Lord.
basic.oneStory: In His last days of temple teaching, Jesus meets every challenge as the rightful Lord, unveiling Himself as the beloved Son the builders reject and God vindicates as cornerstone. The story drives toward the cross, where the tenants will kill the Son, and toward the resurrection and exaltation by which God makes Him the foundation and the Lord.

context.literary:
Luke 20 is a set of five exchanges in the temple courts, and Luke arranges them so that the hostility of the leaders rises and then falls silent. The first is a demand for credentials, verses 1 to 8. The second, the parable of the tenants, is Jesus' answer in story form, verses 9 to 19. Then three attempted traps follow, one political, one theological and one scriptural: the tax question, verses 20 to 26, the resurrection riddle, verses 27 to 40, and Jesus' own question about David's son, verses 41 to 44. A closing warning, verses 45 to 47, turns from the questioners to the crowd.

Each exchange has the same shape. A question is put, Jesus answers or counters, and the questioners end in silence: they could not answer in verse 7, were amazed and fell silent in verse 26, and did not dare to question Him any further in verse 40. By the end Jesus is the one asking, and He asks the only question that cannot be answered without confessing who He is. The movement reverses the opening scene, in which the leaders put the questions.

The parable at the centre carries the passage's argument. Its form follows Isaiah's song of the vineyard, Isaiah 5:1 to 7, but turns it: the problem is not what the vineyard produced but what the tenants did when the owner sent for his share. The three servants of verses 10 to 12 and the one beloved son in verse 13 form a climax in the style of Hebrew narrative, in which the last term stands apart from the series. The parable then moves outward from story to Scripture, as Jesus quotes Psalm 118 in verse 17 and adds a saying about the stone in verse 18, so that a story about a vineyard is turned into a question about the rejected stone.

Luke has placed this chapter between the entry and the temple cleansing of chapter 19 and the Olivet discourse of chapter 21. The leaders who looked for a way to kill Him in 19:47 are now seen working their plan, and the widow of 20:47 prepares for the widow of 21:1 to 4, who gives all she has. Luke uses the final warning to set the contrast between those who devour widows' houses and the widow who gives from her poverty.
context.historical:
The challenge in verse 2 is a question about jurisdiction. The chief priests, scribes and elders made up the Sanhedrin, and they were responsible for the temple. When Jesus entered the courts, drove out the sellers and taught every day, 19:45 to 47, He acted without a permit from them. Their demand to know who gave Him authority was a demand to see His credentials in a place where they believed they held the keys. Jesus' counter-question about John's baptism put them on the horns of a dilemma, because John was popular with the crowd and the leaders had not accepted him.

Vineyards and absentee landowners were a normal part of the Galilean and Judean economy. Tenants paid rent in a share of the produce, and a landowner who lived elsewhere sent agents to collect it. The story does not describe a common situation so much as an extreme one, in which the tenants beat and kill the agents and then the owner's son. The idea of seizing the inheritance by killing the heir seems to assume that the owner is dead or that the land would be treated as ownerless, and Jesus' audience would have heard the improbability as part of the story's shock. They would also have known the vineyard image from Isaiah 5:7, where the vineyard of the LORD is the house of Israel.

The tax question came out of a live political controversy. The census tax of AD 6 had provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean, Acts 5:37, and many Jews felt that paying tribute to Rome was a betrayal of God's kingship. Others, including the supporters of Herod, accepted it. A denarius, the coin Jesus asks to see, bore the head of the emperor and an inscription naming him as son of the divine Augustus, and it was in widespread use. The question was framed so that either answer would bring trouble, with the crowd if Jesus said yes, and with the governor if He said no. The spies hoped to hand Him over to the governor's authority, verse 20, and the later charge before Pilate in 23:2 shows that they did.

The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, centred on the temple, and held only to the five books of Moses. They denied the resurrection and the existence of angels, Acts 23:8. The law of levirate marriage, Deuteronomy 25:5 to 10, required a brother to marry the widow of a childless brother to preserve the family line, and they used it to make the idea of resurrection look absurd. Scribes were the experts in the law, and some of them were Pharisees who believed in the resurrection, which is why they praise Jesus' answer in verse 39.
context.canonical:
The vineyard is one of the great images of Israel in the Old Testament. Isaiah 5:1 to 7 sings of a beloved's vineyard on a fertile hill that yielded wild grapes, and the song explains that the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel. Psalm 80:8 to 16 pictures Israel as a vine brought from Egypt, and Jeremiah 2:21 and Hosea 10:1 use the same figure. Jesus' parable draws on all this, and His audience, the leaders who heard Him in the temple, would have recognised the song of Isaiah in the first line. The change is that the fault now lies with the tenants, the leaders, rather than with the vines.

The servants whom the owner sends are the prophets. The Old Testament tells of the abuse of messengers, in 2 Chronicles 36:15 to 16, where Israel mocked God's messengers until there was no remedy, and in the stoning of Zechariah son of Jehoiada, 2 Chronicles 24:20 to 21. Jesus will say in Luke 11:47 to 51 that this generation is accountable for the blood of the prophets. The beloved son is a new development, and Luke's phrase is the one used of Jesus at His baptism and transfiguration, 3:22 and 9:35.

The stone passage comes from Psalm 118:22, which Jesus quotes in verse 17 with the same psalm that the crowd had sung on the Mount of Olives. The apostles take it up in Acts 4:11, in Peter's address to the Sanhedrin, and in 1 Peter 2:6 to 8, where it is joined with Isaiah 28:16 and 8:14, and in Ephesians 2:20 where Christ is the cornerstone of the household of God. The saying in verse 18, with its picture of breaking and crushing, draws on Isaiah 8:14 to 15 and Daniel 2:34 to 35 and 44 to 45, where a stone strikes the statue of the kingdoms and becomes a mountain that fills the earth.

Jesus' use of Exodus 3:6 echoes the Torah's own testimony to a God who keeps covenant beyond the grave, and it is picked up by Paul, who builds the hope of resurrection into 1 Corinthians 15. The question about David's son depends on Psalm 110:1, which is one of the most often quoted verses of the Old Testament in the New, in Acts 2:34 to 35, Hebrews 1:13 and elsewhere. And the warning about the scribes who devour widows' houses stands in the line of Isaiah 10:1 to 2 and Malachi 3:5, where God judges those who oppress the widow.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see that the rejection of Jesus was not a failure of His method or a surprise to God. The parable says that it was foreseen, and the quotation of the psalm says that it was foretold. He also wants to show that the leaders' hostility was not caused by a lack of evidence. Jesus' authority is demonstrated by His wisdom in each exchange, and what the opponents lack is willingness to hear. When Jesus asks about John's baptism, the leaders will not answer because their answer would expose them, and Luke sets this up as the key to everything that follows.

A second purpose is to show who Jesus is in terms that matter for the church's confession. The beloved son is killed and yet becomes the cornerstone. He is greater than Caesar, for He gives the true account of what belongs to God. He is the one for whom the dead live, because God is the God of the living. And He is David's Lord, seated at God's right hand. These claims prepare for the trial and for the apostolic preaching that He is both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:36.

Luke also has the Gentile reader in mind. The vineyard will be given to others, verse 16, and Theophilus and his fellow believers are among those who have received it. They are not to be proud, for the parable teaches that the vineyard is a trust and not a possession, and the tenants who forgot that lost it. The warning against the scribes in verses 45 to 47 is a reminder that the danger of religious pride is permanent, and that even those who pray at length may be devouring widows.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a series of debates, and the answers Jesus gave are the main thing to carry away, not the debating itself. We are not told that every question must be answered with a counter-question, and the story does not make a rule of Jesus' refusal to say by what authority He acts. He declined because the leaders had not been honest, and He often answered those who sincerely asked.

The tax saying, give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, is recorded as Jesus' answer to a trap. Paul will later say that believers should pay what they owe, taxes to whom taxes are due, Romans 13:7, and Peter that they should honour the emperor, 1 Peter 2:17. So the saying has a lasting application in the Christian's civil obligation. But it is not a charter for the state to claim whatever it likes, because the second half of the saying puts all things under God. It also does not tell us how to apply the principle in every political situation, and Christians have disagreed about its limits. When Caesar's claim contradicts God's, the apostles said we must obey God rather than men, Acts 5:29.

The parable of the tenants is not a command to attack anyone, and its warning of destruction is addressed to a generation who rejected the Son. It has been used in the past to justify contempt for the Jewish people, and that use misreads it. Jesus was a Jew speaking to Jewish leaders, and the first heirs of the vineyard were also Jewish, the apostles themselves. What the chapter asks of us is to receive the Son and to render to God what is His. The warning against the scribes describes what Jesus saw and condemned, and it applies to anyone in religious leadership who uses status and piety for gain.

debates.question: What does the saying about Caesar and God establish?

views.label: A real but limited authority for the state
views.case: The coin carries Caesar's image, so it is his to ask for. Ordinary civic duties such as taxes are legitimate, as Paul will affirm in Romans 13:1 to 7. But the second clause is the weightier one: since human beings bear God's image, Genesis 1:27, they owe Him everything, and Caesar's claim is bounded by God's.

views.label: A shrewd escape that exposes the trap
views.case: Jesus neither endorses nor condemns Roman rule. He shows that His questioners carry Caesar's coin, and so they are already part of the system they are trying to use against Him. The saying lifts the question above the level of politics and gives no formula for the state.

views.label: A challenge about whose image we are
views.case: The word image is the word used for humanity in the Greek of Genesis 1:27. On this reading Jesus is hinting that the real coin to be handed to God is the person who bears His image, which means that the saying is about total allegiance rather than about taxes.

debates.bearing: The first two readings agree that taxes may be paid, and the third adds the depth of the second clause. Luke 23:2 shows that the leaders later reported Jesus as forbidding tribute, which shows that He had not done so.

debates.question: What is the cornerstone, and what is meant by the stone that crushes?

views.label: The foundation stone laid at the corner
views.case: The phrase kephale gonias, head of the corner, is read as the stone laid first at the foundation, on which the walls are aligned. The apostles use it so, Ephesians 2:20, and the picture is of Christ as the foundation of the new temple.

views.label: The capstone at the top
views.case: Others take the head of the corner as the stone that finishes an arch or the top of a building. The saying about a stone that falls and crushes in verse 18 fits a stone from above, and the picture is of Christ exalted after rejection.

debates.bearing: Both pictures describe a rejected stone given the highest honour. The saying in verse 18 says that every person meets the stone in one of two ways, by stumbling on it and being broken, or by being struck by it in judgment. The call is to fall on it now in repentance.

debates.question: How does Jesus prove the resurrection from the burning bush?

views.label: An argument from the living God
views.case: If God says I am the God of Abraham centuries after Abraham died, then Abraham must still be alive to God, who is the God of the living. The Sadducees accepted only the Torah, and Jesus answers from the Torah. The argument rests on the covenant relationship God keeps with His people beyond death.

views.label: A rabbinic style of reasoning from a text
views.case: Some see here a form of argument from the tense and force of a single statement, familiar in Jewish debate. The point is not that the verse states the resurrection outright but that it implies it, as the covenant promise requires that those to whom it was made share in its fulfilment.

debates.bearing: Luke adds that to God all are alive, verse 38, which makes the covenant argument the main thing. The hope of resurrection does not rest on a proof text but on the character of the God who made promises to people and will not break them.

study.originalLanguages:
The question of verse 2 hinges on exousia, authority, the right to act and the power to carry it out. The leaders ask what kind of exousia Jesus has and who gave it. Jesus' counter-question about John's baptism is a clever one because the answer would be the same: from heaven. The same word returns in the Gospel's earlier scenes, 4:32 and 36 and 5:24, where Jesus teaches with authority and forgives with authority. The leaders have no way to answer because to say from heaven would indict them.

In the parable the key figure is the agapetos, beloved son, in verse 13. The adjective is the one used by the voice from heaven at the baptism and transfiguration, 3:22 and 9:35, so the reader hears the parable as a story about Jesus Himself. The owner's reasoning, Perhaps they will respect him, uses a word that expresses a hope rather than a certainty, and it shows a patience that goes beyond what one would expect. The tenants' words in verse 14 use kleronomia, inheritance, the same noun that the rich ruler hoped to inherit in 18:18 as the verb kleronomeo. Those who try to seize the inheritance lose it, and those who receive it as a gift gain it.

Luke says the son was thrown out of the vineyard and then killed, verse 15, where Mark has the opposite order. The order fits the death of Jesus outside the city, which Hebrews 13:12 notes. The people's response in verse 16, me genoito, may it never be, is the same emphatic rejection that Paul will use repeatedly in Romans. Only Luke records it, and it shows that the crowd understood the parable's meaning, even if they could not accept it.

The quotation in verse 17 uses kephale gonias, literally head of the corner. The meaning, whether foundation or capstone, is debated, but the force is the same, a stone of the highest importance. The verbs in verse 18, synthlasthesetai, will be broken to pieces, and likmesei, will crush, can mean to winnow or to crush to powder, and they give two different fates to the person who meets the stone.

In the tax question, the questioners flatter Jesus with the words that you speak and teach correctly, and Luke calls them spies, enkathetoi, those who lie in wait. Jesus asks for a denarius and uses the word eikon, image, which is the word for human beings made in God's image in the Greek of Genesis 1:27. His command uses apodote, give back, which implies that something is owed. Paul uses the same verb in Romans 13:7 when he says give to everyone what you owe them.

The Sadducees' question puts anastasis, resurrection, at the centre. Jesus speaks of the age to come, and says that those counted worthy to attain it, kataxiothentes, neither marry nor die, being like angels and sons of God, huioi theou, because they are sons of the resurrection. The word worthy here does not mean earned: it is the word for being counted worthy, as in Acts 5:41. In verse 42 the quotation of Psalm 110:1 uses kyrios twice, the LORD said to my Lord, which in the Greek version represents the divine name and a title of honour. David calls his descendant kyrios, and the question is how the son can be Lord.

typology.type: The vineyard and its tenants, Luke 20:9 to 16
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 5:1 to 7 describes the vineyard of the LORD as Israel, planted and tended with care and yielding bad fruit. Jesus carries the picture forward: the owner has sent servants, the prophets, and then His Son. The correspondence is that Israel's leaders again fail to give the owner what is His. The escalation in Christ is that the Son Himself is killed outside the vineyard, and the vineyard is given to others, which Peter applies to the new people of God, 1 Peter 2:9 to 10. In John 15:1 Jesus is Himself the true vine, so the vine is not only a people but a person in whom a new Israel grows. The type falls short in that the parable ends in judgment, whereas the cross opens a door for the tenants as well, Acts 6:7.

Psalm 118:22 speaks of a stone the builders rejected, which became the chief cornerstone. In its first setting, the psalm celebrates a deliverance of the king or the nation that the nations had despised. Jesus applies it to Himself, and Peter preaches it to the rulers who condemned Him, Acts 4:10 to 11. Isaiah 8:14 describes a stone of stumbling, and Isaiah 28:16 a tested stone laid in Zion, and Peter combines them in 1 Peter 2:4 to 8. The correspondence is that the one who was rejected is the foundation of God's house, and the escalation is that He is also raised from death. The type is still open in that the stone will fall in final judgment on those who do not receive it, Daniel 2:44 to 45 and Matthew 21:44.

typology.type: The Lord who sits at God's right hand, Luke 20:41 to 44
typology.fulfillment: Psalm 110 is the royal psalm in which David hears the LORD speak to his Lord and promise to make his enemies a footstool. In its original setting it addresses the king who will rule from Zion and who is also a priest in the order of Melchizedek, verse 4. Jesus uses it to show that the Messiah is more than David's son. Peter says that David did not ascend into heaven, so the psalm speaks of the risen Jesus, Acts 2:34 to 36, and Hebrews 1:13 and 10:12 to 13 apply it to His enthronement. The type reaches full strength in Christ, who is both David's offspring and David's Lord, Romans 1:3 to 4, and the psalm has not yet reached its end, for the enemies are not yet all subdued, 1 Corinthians 15:25.

typology.type: The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Luke 20:37 to 38
typology.fulfillment: God revealed Himself to Moses at the bush as the God of the fathers, Exodus 3:6, and the promises He made to them were of land, descendants and blessing. Jesus draws out the implication that the God who spoke to Moses is still their God, so that the fathers are alive to Him. Hebrews 11:13 to 16 says that these patriarchs died in faith without receiving the promises, and that God has prepared a city for them. The correspondence is that the covenant looks beyond death. The escalation is Christ's own resurrection, the first fruits of those who have died, 1 Corinthians 15:20, which makes the argument a fact.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by answering the first question put to Him. The leaders ask who gave Him authority, and the whole of the chapter is His reply. He does not produce a certificate. He tells a story in which He is the beloved son, the heir whom the tenants kill, and He says that the owner's patient sending of servants culminates in the sending of the only one who is truly His. The word beloved connects the story to the voice at the Jordan and on the mountain, so that Luke's reader hears the Father confirming what the leaders refuse to see. The authority He claims is not borrowed from the temple. It is the authority of the Son.

He is also the stone. The picture in verse 17 turns the story of rejection into a story of vindication. The builders reject, God makes the stone the cornerstone, and the stone then judges those who will not receive it. Peter quoted this to the Sanhedrin, Acts 4:11, and tells believers that the stone is precious to those who believe, 1 Peter 2:7. The rejection is therefore part of the plan, and the resurrection is the proof that God has reversed the verdict of the leaders.

In answering the Sadducees, Jesus speaks of the resurrection as a settled fact of the age to come, and He speaks as one who will accomplish it. He will be the first to rise, Acts 26:23, and those who are sons of the resurrection are sons because of Him. In Romans 1:4 Paul says that He was declared to be the Son of God with power by the resurrection from the dead. The God of the living is the God who will raise His Son and those who are in Him.

The last question is the most direct. Jesus asks how the Christ can be David's son when David calls Him Lord. He does not answer it in the chapter, and He leaves the question hanging in the air for the reader to answer. The answer is that He is both, the offspring of David according to the flesh, and the Lord who sits at God's right hand, Romans 1:3 to 4. Peter will give the answer on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:36, and Jesus Himself will speak of sitting at the right hand of the power of God before the Sanhedrin, Luke 22:69.

Even the tax saying points to Him. The image on the coin is Caesar's, but the image that the human being bears is God's, and Christ is the one who is the image of the invisible God, Colossians 1:15. The perfect human, who renders to God everything, is the only one who can restore the image in us, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The warning here is not to turn the coin into a code. The saying is first a reply to a trap, and its connection to Christ is the unity of His own allegiance: He gave God everything, and He taught that Caesar's due is to be paid.
study.god:
The parable gives a picture of God that is hard and beautiful at once. The owner is a landowner who has given the vineyard to tenants and gone away, which can look like absence, but his repeated sending of servants is persistence. He keeps coming for what is his and he keeps giving the tenants another chance. When he sends the son, he says Perhaps they will respect him, which is the language of a father taking a risk out of love. This is the God of Ezekiel 18:23 who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and of 2 Peter 3:9 who is patient, not wanting any to perish. And the verdict at the end is real. The one who gives and gives is also the one who comes, and the parable says the owner will kill the tenants and give the vineyard to others. The patience of God is not unlimited indulgence.

God is also shown as the one who owns everything. The vineyard is his, and the tenants are stewards. This is the theology of Psalm 24:1 and of Haggai 2:8, the earth is the LORD's, and everything in it. That is what is behind Jesus' saying about giving to God what is God's. If we are made in His image, then He has a claim on us that no earthly power can match. The coin belongs to Caesar, but the person belongs to God. This does not deprive the state of its role, Romans 13:1, but it limits it, and every human power answers to the God who gave it.

The answer to the Sadducees reveals that God is a God of the living. He does not make covenant promises to people and then abandon them to dust. His fidelity extends past death. The statement that to Him all are alive means that every person who has died is still before God, and that His relationship to them has not ended. The God of the burning bush is the same who raises the dead, and that is the ground of Christian hope.

The last exchange shows that God is Father to a Son who is Lord. The LORD says to my Lord: the doctrine of the Trinity is not worked out in the passage, but the psalm Jesus quotes has two figures, and the New Testament sees in this the Father and the Son. The way God has set the Son at His right hand, with enemies as a footstool, shows a God whose purposes will be carried out and whose King will reign.

For worship this means we approach God as His tenants, with gratitude for what we have been given and the knowledge that we hold it on trust. We bring Him the fruit that He asks for, and we give Him ourselves, for we bear His image. We praise Him as the God who is faithful to the dead and living alike, and we acknowledge the Son whom He has made Lord. And we take heart that the stone He has laid will stand, whatever the builders say.

crossReferences.note: The song of the vineyard describes the beloved's care for his vine and its wild grapes, and Isaiah explains that the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel. Jesus' hearers knew this song, and the parable of the tenants takes its setting from it. The turn is that Isaiah blames the vine, while Jesus blames the tenants who will not give the owner his fruit.

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and the psalmist says that this is the LORD's doing and marvellous in our eyes. Jesus quotes the verse in Luke 20:17 immediately after the parable, applying it to the killing of the son. The vindication that follows rejection is God's own work, which is the answer to the leaders' plan.

The LORD of hosts will be a sanctuary, but also a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to both houses of Israel, and many will stumble and fall and be broken. Jesus' saying in Luke 20:18 about those who fall on the stone and are broken reflects this passage. The same God is a refuge to those who trust Him and a stumbling-block to those who do not.

A stone cut without hands strikes the statue of the kingdoms, crushes it to dust and becomes a great mountain that fills the earth. The image of the stone that crushes in Luke 20:18 recalls this. It shows that the stone Jesus speaks of is not only a rejected stone but the beginning of a kingdom that will outlast every other.

The law of levirate marriage requires a man to take his dead brother's childless widow to raise up a name for his brother. The Sadducees' story in Luke 20:28 builds on this commandment. The law was meant to preserve a family and its inheritance in Israel, and it assumed the present age. Jesus answers that the age to come is not governed by such arrangements.

At the burning bush the LORD says to Moses, I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. This is the text Jesus uses in Luke 20:37. It is a statement made long after the patriarchs had died, which leads Jesus to say that God is the God of the living. The text is chosen because the Sadducees accepted the Torah and no other part of Scripture.

The LORD says to David's Lord, Sit at My right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet, and the same psalm adds a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. Jesus' question in Luke 20:41 to 44 draws attention to the puzzle of the first verse. The New Testament answers that the Messiah is David's son and David's Lord, enthroned at God's right hand.

Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, tells the rulers and elders that the man was healed by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised from the dead. He then quotes the stone psalm, saying that salvation is found in no one else. It is the first apostolic use of the saying Jesus gave in Luke 20:17, delivered to the very court that rejected Him.

Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, since there is no authority except from God, and to give everyone what is owed, taxes to whom taxes are owed. It is the apostolic application of the saying about Caesar. The key is that authority is God's gift, which both grounds the duty of paying taxes and sets a limit on what the state may claim.

Woe to those who make unjust laws, to deprive the poor of their rights and rob the widows of their due. Jesus' charge in Luke 20:47 that the scribes devour widows' houses stands in the prophetic line. Religious learning does not excuse the exploitation of the vulnerable, and long prayers do not cover it. The widow of 21:1 to 4 in the next scene is the counter-picture.

study.oneStory:
The vineyard stands in a story that begins with a garden. God planted a garden in Eden and put the man in it to work it and take care of it, Genesis 2:15, giving him everything but one tree and the warning not to take what was not his. The fall was a seizure: they reached for what had not been given, and were driven out. The parable of the tenants replays the original sin on a larger stage. Tenants who have been given a vineyard treat it as their own, and the owner's messengers meet violence. The heir is killed so that the inheritance can be taken. It is Genesis 3 and Genesis 4 together, the grasping for what belongs to God and the murder that follows.

The Old Testament is the history of the sending of servants. Moses and the prophets were sent to Israel, and they were often beaten, imprisoned and killed. God kept sending them because He loved His people, and 2 Chronicles 36:15 says He had compassion on them. The parable looks back over that whole history in three strokes and then moves to what is unique, the sending of the beloved son. The line of the story goes from Abel, the first righteous man killed, to Zechariah son of Jehoiada, and then to the Son who is killed outside the vineyard. In Him the long story of rejection reaches its end and its reversal.

Because the Son is raised, the stone is made the cornerstone. The temple that Jesus teaches in is under judgment, and a new house is rising on the stone that was rejected. Peter says that believers are living stones built into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5, and Paul says that Gentiles are no longer strangers but fellow citizens built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:19 to 20. The vineyard given to others is this new people, drawn from Jews and Gentiles, who are given the vineyard because they are united to the Son.

The questions that follow place Jesus in the larger story as well. The tax question asks whose image we bear, and goes back to the creation of humanity in God's image. The resurrection question looks forward to the age to come, when death is undone, and the God of the burning bush is vindicated. The question about David's son points to the enthronement of the Messiah in the psalm, and to the day when all enemies are made a footstool.

The story ends in the new creation, where the tenants are no longer rebellious and the King reigns. In Revelation 21 and 22 the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life is there for the healing of the nations. The inheritance that the tenants tried to seize is given freely to the sons of the resurrection. Those who are worthy of the age to come neither marry nor die, and they see the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob face to face, Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: How does Jesus respond to the demand to know His authority?

options.text: He asks whether John's baptism was from heaven or men, trapping His challengers and declining to answer them.
options.note: Luke 20:3-8 shows the counter-question that exposes their bad faith.

options.text: He turns the question back on them with a question of His own.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific question about John and its exposing effect.

options.text: He explains in detail that His authority comes from God.
options.note: He does not spell it out; He exposes their evasion instead.

options.text: He admits He has no authority to act as He does.
options.note: He never concedes this; He implies a heavenly authority they will not acknowledge.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the wicked tenants reveal?

options.text: The leaders reject the beloved Son as the tenants kill the heir, but God makes the rejected stone the cornerstone.
options.note: Luke 20:9-17 casts the leaders as tenants and Jesus as the rejected, exalted stone.

options.text: The tenants killed the owner's son to seize the inheritance.
options.note: True to the story, but it omits the identification of Jesus as the rejected cornerstone.

options.text: God is patient with His vineyard for a long time.
options.note: His patience is shown, but the point is the rejection of the Son and God's vindication of Him.

options.text: The tenants were justified in keeping the vineyard.
options.note: They are condemned; the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by 'give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's'?

options.text: The state has a real but limited claim, while God, whose image we bear, claims all of life.
options.note: Luke 20:24-25 grants Caesar his coin yet asserts God's total claim.

options.text: It is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar.
options.note: True, but it omits the weightier claim of God over the whole of our lives.

options.text: Religion and government must never touch each other.
options.note: Jesus distinguishes their claims but subordinates all to God, not a strict separation.

options.text: We owe Caesar nothing at all.
options.note: He affirms that Caesar's due should be rendered to him.

quiz.q: How does Jesus prove the resurrection to the Sadducees?

options.text: From Moses: God calls Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and He is the God of the living.
options.note: Luke 20:37-38 argues from Exodus that the patriarchs live to God.

options.text: He shows that God keeps His covenant beyond death.
options.note: True in substance, but it omits the specific proof from the burning bush that they accepted.

options.text: He appeals to the prophets' promises of new life.
options.note: He argues from Moses, whom the Sadducees accepted, not from the prophets.

options.text: He admits the resurrection cannot be proven from Scripture.
options.note: The opposite: He proves it directly from Moses.

quiz.q: What point does Jesus make about the Christ and David?

options.text: David calls the Christ his Lord in Psalm 110, so the Messiah is more than David's son; He is David's Lord.
options.note: Luke 20:41-44 shows the Christ is David's Lord, pointing to His divine exaltation.

options.text: The Christ is descended from David.
options.note: True and assumed, but Jesus' point is that He is also David's Lord, greater than a mere son.

options.text: David wrote many psalms about the Messiah.
options.note: The specific point is the title 'Lord' in Psalm 110, not David's authorship in general.

options.text: The Christ has nothing to do with David.
options.note: Jesus affirms the Christ is David's son, while showing He is also David's Lord.

questions: The leaders demanded Jesus' credentials but would not submit to His authority. Where do you question God's right to rule a part of your life you would rather keep for yourself?
The tenants wanted the vineyard without the owner and killed the Son to get it. In what ways are you tempted to want God's gifts while resisting His claim on you?
Jesus said to render to God what bears His image, and you bear it. What would it mean to give God not just a slice of your life but the whole of it?
The Sadducees could not imagine resurrection because they underestimated God. Where has a small view of God shrunk your hope, and how does the God of the living enlarge it?
Jesus warned against religion done for show while widows were devoured. Where might your outward devotion be masking neglect of the vulnerable or a love of being seen?

translationNotes.note: The question 'John's baptism, was it from heaven, or from men?' is a trap that exposes the leaders' unwillingness to judge honestly.

Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the stone the builders rejected becoming the cornerstone, applying the Scripture to His own rejection and vindication. The image becomes central to the apostles' preaching in Acts and the epistles.

Verse 30 is very brief, 'Then the second', because some later manuscripts expand it with a repeated clause about the brother marrying and dying. The BSB follows the shorter earliest text; the meaning of the Sadducees' riddle is unaffected.
